books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence
Madison's Presidency and the War of 1812

stimulus.text:
Henry Clay, a congressman from Kentucky, spoke in the House of Representatives on January 22, 1812, urging the United States to build up its navy:

“Sir, if you wish to avoid foreign commerce; give up all your prosperity. It is the thing protected, not the instrument of protection, that involves you in war. Commerce engenders collision, collision war, and war, the argument supposes, leads to despotism. Would the councils of that statesman be deemed who would recommend that the nation should be unarmed—that in the art of war, the material spirit, and martial exercises, should be prohibited—and that the great body of the people should be taught that the national happiness was to be found in perpetual peace alone? No, sir.”
stimulus.source_note: Henry Clay, Speech on the Increase of the Navy, House of Representatives, January 22, 1812; wording verified against Wikiquote's sourced text. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Clay's speech was most directly aimed at critics who argued that

options.text: the United States should stay unarmed and accept peace at any price
the United States should invade Canada immediately
options.misconception: War Hawks wanted Canada; Clay was one of them, not their critic.

options.text: the Embargo Act of 1807 should be made permanent law
options.misconception: The embargo had already failed and been repealed in 1809.

options.text: the United States should form an alliance with France against Britain
options.misconception: No one in Congress was pushing a French alliance in 1812.

rationales.A: Clay asks whether any wise statesman would recommend that the nation be unarmed and its people taught that happiness lies in perpetual peace alone. His answer, “No, sir,” is aimed at exactly those critics.
rationales.B: Invading Canada was the War Hawks' own goal. Clay shared it, so he would not argue against it.
rationales.C: The Embargo Act was repealed in 1809, three years before this speech. Nobody in 1812 was arguing to make it permanent.
rationales.D: France was also seizing American ships, and no faction in Congress wanted a French alliance. Clay's target was the peace-at-any-price argument.
rationales.general:
1. Find his question. He asks whether a wise statesman would tell the nation to stay unarmed and seek peace alone.
2. Find his answer. “No, sir.” He rejects that advice outright.
3. Put it together. The speech answers people who said the United States should disarm and accept whatever Britain did.
Background: Clay spoke in January 1812, six months before Congress declared war, while Madison was still holding out for a peaceful answer.
Remember: when a speaker asks a question and answers it himself, the question tells you who he is arguing against.
